# Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness and Hybrid Mind Uploading

By Daniel Burger. https://consciousness.ink/

## Glossary

### Synthetic consciousness

The vision of this series: consciousness that no longer has to end, starting with the consciousness that exists now. Summarised in 0/30 as "engineered phenomenology on a designed substrate you could gradually become". "Synthetic" says that the result is the real kind of consciousness, reached via a creation process; the series calls a consciousness synthetic once it is sustained by created and engineered parts. It is used differently from "artificial consciousness" and "machine consciousness", which 1/30 discusses.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#synthetic-consciousness

### Hybrid mind uploading (HMU)

The mission of this series and the route to synthetic consciousness. Rather than creating something external to the brain that recreates the brain, it builds something that can be integrated into the brain itself. "Hybrid" means that biological and engineered parts carry one and the same process at the same time: what is hybrid is the thing that carries consciousness, never the consciousness itself. It works by non-destructive co-running and gradual replacement, and is distinguished from classical mind uploading, which treats a copy as survival.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#hybrid-mind-uploading

### Classical mind uploading (CMU)

The name this series uses for mind uploading via whole brain emulation: scan a brain in as much detail as possible, store it, and then simulate it in order to emulate consciousness on a different substrate, a computer. Some versions are fully destructive. The series does not treat a separate instance reconstructed this way as the survival of the original consciousness.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#classical-mind-uploading

### Mind uploading

The broader idea whose original goals were solving death, mind augmentation and enabling a new state of humanity, popularised in the Hans Moravec lineage. The series keeps the term for what it promises and drops its old method, splitting it into classical and hybrid mind uploading.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#mind-uploading

### Whole brain emulation (WBE)

The academic name for the scan-and-simulate approach to mind uploading, which 2/30 traces to Randal Koene around 1998. In this series, mind uploading via whole brain emulation is what is called classical mind uploading.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#whole-brain-emulation

### Process world-line

The 4D trajectory of the physical-dynamical and organised bounded processes going on in your head that constitute what we call your brain. It is a physical claim about the process that does the carrying, not a report of how continuous it feels, since a copy would feel continuous too. In this series, death is the irreversible end of the process world-line.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#process-world-line

### Gradual brain replacement

Swapping the brain's substrate out piece by piece without destroying the physical-dynamical and organised bounded processes, ideally while adding repairability and fault tolerance, so that the process world-line hardens and becomes more resilient. It is the replacement side of hybrid mind uploading.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#gradual-brain-replacement

### Mechanistic gradual brain replacement (MGBR)

Named in 3/30 as the core of hybrid mind uploading, and as step one towards solving death, after functional brain isolation. 0/30 says that a different piece of brain can take over a function, but that a different substrate taking over is still open and is the reason for the replacement work. 3/30 says whether a world-line truly went on via a replacement has to be shown physically.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#mechanistic-gradual-brain-replacement

### Serial lesion effect

Cited in 0/30, together with Barrett's (2013) gradual reorganisation principle: a different piece of brain can take over a function. What neither of them gives you, the post says, is a different substrate taking over, which is still open.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#serial-lesion-effect

### Gradual reorganisation principle

Barrett's (2013) principle, cited in 0/30 together with the serial lesion effect: a different piece of brain can take over a function. What neither of them gives you, the post says, is a different substrate taking over, which is still open.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#gradual-reorganisation-principle

### Solving death

The goal that no one has to end, which is different from halting the natural process of dying. Reversing ageing halts the dying but does not solve death, since you can still get hit by a bus. The goal says "no one has to end", never "no one is allowed to end", because only a continuation worth having counts. In the Ontology it is one of the three hard goals the mission has to achieve; functional brain isolation is step zero towards it, and gradual replacement comes after. Solved means the remaining risk keeps falling fast enough that all the yearly risks add up to a finite total.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#solving-death

### Functional brain isolation

Taking a living brain out of its body and keeping it alive outside of it for as long as possible, the work of Eightsix: early success in rodents, work towards a large animal brain, and ultimately humans. In this series it is step zero on the route to solving death, before gradual replacement.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#functional-brain-isolation

### Deprivation view of death

Nagel's view, used in 3/30 as the central reason why death is bad: death is the irreversible end of a conscious process world-line, so everything that would have come after does not happen for the someone that this world-line is, and if that would have been worth having, missing out on it is bad for that someone.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#deprivation-view

### Adaptive preferences

Elster's term, also called "sour grapes", used in 3/30 for making your peace with death because, for basically all of human history, there was nothing anybody could do about it. The post says that the wish to solve death can be explained away, but so can everybody else's acceptance, and that explaining away doesn't decide anything.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#adaptive-preferences

### Genetic fallacy

Used in 3/30 for treating the causes of wanting to solve death (an upbringing, a teenage bookshelf) as if they showed that the goal itself is bad. The post distinguishes a cause (what made you want it) from a reason (what makes it worth wanting): those stories tell you how he ended up with death as his main topic, but they don't tell you at all if the goal itself is any good, and they also can't tell you that it's bad.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#genetic-fallacy

### Death

The irreversible end of a conscious process world-line; seen from the engineering side, the irreversible destruction of the physical and dynamic processes of consciousness. "Irreversible" is meant strictly: the end that cannot be undone by anything that physics allows. Medicine keeps pushing the point where a stop turns into an end further out, so solving death is never about bringing somebody back from an end, only about never letting a stop turn into one.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#death

### Amortality

What you get when the dying is halted (ageing, failing organs): no clock in you runs out by itself anymore. It is step zero, not solving death, since a risk that just stays where it is, like being hit by a bus, still gets everybody in the end, only later.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#amortality

### Immortality

The state in which death cannot occur at all anymore. In the order "stop dying and achieve amortality, then solve death and seek immortality", it is something one can seek once death is solved, and not part of the goal.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#immortality

### Understand consciousness

The second of the three goals of the Ontology. "Understand" comes in three levels: measuring it, modelling it and explaining it. The goal counts as reached at the second level, a model that can tell you before a replacement step if the experience will change; the third is the horizon, and it may never be reachable by science. It is ordered second because it is what is needed to check that death really got solved: hybrid mind uploading can sidestep a theory of consciousness when building the thing that carries the process, but it cannot sidestep measuring.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#understand-consciousness

### Measurement theory

The most modest of the three: it only tells you what kind of data count at all (reports, behaviour, neural markers, and so on) and how to read that data as experience; it doesn't say why. In this series, measurement comes first, before a full theory, with the two correcting each other in turns, because what you think consciousness is already shapes what you accept as a measurement of it.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#measurement-theory

### Model of consciousness

With a model you can already predict which experience goes with which physical state. In this series it is the second of three levels of "understand" (measure, model, explain), and the level at which the goal counts as reached: a model that allows us to measure, predict and steer experience across a replacement step, and that can tell you before a step you cannot undo whether the experience will change.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#model-of-consciousness

### Theory of consciousness

A theory would say what consciousness is and why there is any of it in the first place. 4/30 treats this as the third level of "understand", the horizon, and worries that it may belong with questions science cannot settle, so that a theory of consciousness may always be poetry in Bohr's sense. Hybrid mind uploading does not let its success depend on any single theory of consciousness being the only true one; rival theories become predictions that a measurement can test.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#theory-of-consciousness

### Goal vs outcome

A goal is something that we strive for and could fail at; an outcome is what follows either way, as long as we work on the mission. Understanding consciousness is a goal, at least up to the level of measurement, and not a mere outcome, because without a way to tell that experience is still there, and that it's still this experience, we could never know if the mission succeeded. 5/30 applies the distinction to transcending humanity: the capability could become possible while nobody goes beyond a limit, or while the minds that do are all replacements. The goal is that we get there as the ones that we are.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#goal-vs-outcome

### Consciousness engineering

Engineering with matter that we try to couple and integrate with the biological brain, so that experience extends across both parts ("bridging" phenomenal consciousness), with the aim of ultimately letting it host synthetic consciousness. 4/30 uses this name both for that work and for the Frontiers Research Topic Daniel co-organised, and contrasts it with consciousness science: an engineering mindset rather than a science mindset, though the measurement problem of consciousness may be solved from this work.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#consciousness-engineering

### Biomimetic neuromorphics

The slot that whole brain emulation has in classical mind uploading, but in hybrid mind uploading. 4/30 expects measurement theories, and maybe even models of consciousness, to emerge from this work, and treats a good model of consciousness here as useful enough to say that we understand consciousness.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#biomimetic-neuromorphics

### Sidestepping

What hybrid mind uploading does with a theory of consciousness: it does not need a theory in order to make the work succeed, or to have confidence in it, but it does not ignore theories either. Ignoring them completely would be insanity, as you'd end up assuming one anyway. Sidestepping means hybrid mind uploading doesn't let its success depend on any single theory of consciousness being the only true one; it assumes a few things openly (the process world-line is one, held as a hypothesis), and rival theories become predictions that a measurement can test.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#sidestepping

### Adversarial collaboration

Named in 4/30 as one of the first signs of a rigorisation of the consciousness sciences: theories with conflicting predictions get tested against each other.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#adversarial-collaboration

### Inventing Temperature

Hasok Chang's example, used in 4/30: thermometers and fixed scales (Fahrenheit, 1724) were around long before a kinetic theory explained what temperature is (1850s–1870s). You can't calibrate a thermometer without knowing what temperature really is, and you can't know what temperature is without a thermometer, so every round of measuring corrected the concept, and also the other way around. This is the picture for how a measurement theory and a theory of consciousness correct each other in turns.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#inventing-temperature

### Transcend humanity

The third and last of the three goals of the Ontology, and the transformative one, where the thing that changes is us. Until 5/30 it was called "human transcendence". It means going beyond the limits that human biology sets for us, and only those: the limits that physics sets stay where they are. What gets left behind is the species, the kind we were born into with the limits of its biology, not the person who goes beyond them, not the people who would rather stay, and not being humane. It has to stay you, and it does not have to stay human. In terms of the process world-line, it is what lets that same world-line outgrow the limits that it was born with. It comes last because it needs both the engineered carrier that solving death brings and more understanding of consciousness than solving death does.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#transcend-humanity

### Limits of biology

The limits that come from the thing that carries us, which came with the biology that we were born into. Death is the one that everybody knows. 5/30 names others: what we can experience (vision is roughly one octave of the electromagnetic spectrum), what we can keep (memory compresses what it stores and rebuilds what it recalls), how much a mind can hold, where a mind can exist, and being one mind, closed off from every other one. A telescope, a notebook or a spacesuit go around a limit and leave it where it was, in the thing that carries the experience. They are distinct from the limits that physics sets, which stay where they are, and from the adumbrations of perception, which hold for any mind.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#limits-of-biology

### Adumbrations

Husserl's term (Ideas I, §§41–44), as read in 5/30: walking around a table, I only ever see it from one side at a time, so the table is always "more" than what is given right now, whereas the seeing itself is immanent and does not come in sides. The table is not a thing-in-itself behind its appearances; its transcendence lies in how it is given, which is never completely. Husserl says this holds for any mind that perceives a thing, even for God, so transcending humanity does not try to get rid of it. What can change is how much of that "more" a mind gets to.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#adumbrations

### Transhumanism

The position that it is possible and desirable to use technology in order to go beyond the limits of human biology, up to a point where the result may be called posthuman, in the transhumanist sense of a being with capacities far beyond ours (not the "posthumanism" of the humanities). Julian Huxley made the word known in the 1950s, with "man remaining man, but transcending himself", meant for the species as a whole. 5/30 starts with the single someone instead and drops the "remaining man". The goal is not called transhumanism because an -ism is something that you hold, and a goal is something that you reach, or don't.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#transhumanism

### Steerable phenomenology

A carrier that gets built, rather than born, can be built differently: a built substrate is a steerable one. With every gradual replacement step there is a bit of the carrier that does not have to repeat every limit of the tissue that it replaced, and where there is freedom like this the substrate becomes steerable, and with it, bit by bit, the phenomenology. Earlier described as the thing that the transhumanist has long dreamt of without once having thought it.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#steerable-phenomenology

### Lossless Q-storage

From an unpublished working document of January 2026, "Synthetic Substrates and the Destruction of the Forward Arrow of Personal Time", which leans on Lyre's neurophenomenal structuralism. The "Q" stands for what an experience is like. The thesis is that the losses of memory are a contingent limit of biological storage, not a principled one: a substrate that stored an experience whole would give a memory as rich as the experience and the same at every recall, a personal time one can traverse. There is no guarantee that it can be built, and it involves no time travel, since only the playback changes and the substrate still runs forward. In the Ontology it sits under augmented cognition.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#lossless-q-storage

### World-line fidelity

5/30 states the Ontology's rule: the process world-line never breaks, and nothing gets traded against it, enhancement included. A great deal may change, but there cannot be a moment at which one stops and another takes over. At every step it has to be still you, the "continuer", not a promise that you stay the way you are, or about where you end up. That the world-line really goes on through such changes is a hypothesis.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#world-line-fidelity

### Substrate independence

The first of the three outcomes of the Ontology, listed as a state: mind no longer tied to biological substrate. It pairs with the goal of solving death: gradual replacement brings a carrier that is no longer the biology that we were born with. It is an outcome, not a goal, as it comes along with the work, and it was never meant as a guarantee, since how far it can go is decided by physics. 6/30 rejects the reading in which the substrate simply does not matter and keeps only the two words: what it means by them is the re-creation of the brain's constraints in another material, which it calls physical substrate independence.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#substrate-independence

### Computational substrate independence

What Bostrom and classical mind uploading mean by substrate independence: a mind depends only on the computation, so whatever runs it will do. Bostrom wrote "substrate-independence" into his 2003 simulation argument, introducing it as "a common assumption in the philosophy of mind". 6/30 recounts how, in May 2026, the series filed it under the commitments that fix the answers in advance.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#computational-substrate-independence

### Physical substrate independence

What the series means by substrate independence: a mind depends on what its carrier physically does, so whatever does the same will do, be it biological or not. What it is supposed to become independent of is biology, and physics it never leaves. It claims less than the computational version, as a material that does the same physics also runs the same computation along the way, but not the other way round. Whether any material other than living cells can do the job is a question for experiments.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#physical-substrate-independence

### Multiple realisability

Putnam's argument in "Psychological Predicates" (1967): pain cannot be one particular state of the brain, as an octopus presumably feels pain with a brain built very differently, so pain has to be a functional state that many kinds of matter can realise. 6/30 starts instead from an observation within humans: we have somewhat the same kind of experience although our brains all differ, and slow-growing gliomas show living neural tissue taking over from living neural tissue. In that bio-to-bio sense (weak multiple realisability) it is evidenced; whether a different kind of substrate can take over is still open.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#multiple-realisability

### Medium independence

Gualtiero Piccinini's term: a computation does not care what its vehicles are made of, as long as they have the right degrees of freedom. He contrasts it with multiple realisability, via the mousetrap, which can be built in many ways but still has to catch actual mice. 6/30: classical mind uploading turned out to need medium independence for minds, while the series needs at most multiple realisability, as in the heart-lung machine, whose "lung" is a bundle of plastic fibres.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#medium-independence

### Augmented cognition

The second outcome of the Ontology. 7/30 uses it neither in DARPA's sense (a programme from the early 2000s about computers that adapt to the measured cognitive state of their user) nor in Engelbart's (1962) sense of better tools around a person, but for expanding the normal baseline of human cognition, and of conscious experience, which the name does not say. It is the bet that if a mind sits on a carrier that we built, the phenomenal space itself becomes steerable, not only the tools around it. Whatever takes what somebody can experience or do outside the range that they had before is called augmentation. In the Ontology's order it comes late, after preservation.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#augmented-cognition

### Baseline first

7/30: not to start from an augmented state as step one. First the same constraints, then changes to them, one at a time, and never both at once, with augmentation last. The baseline means the person's own, so how they experienced things and what they could do before, and no norm of what a human should be. It only shows what changed: that it is still the same someone hangs on the process having gone on, not on anybody's report. The baseline does not have to be better; it only has to come first.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#baseline-first

### Comparison and verification problem

7/30's main objection to classical mind uploading and whole brain emulation: scanned, emulated and switched on, the substrate, the body, the surroundings and probably the capacities all change in one step. Whoever comes out has no before of their own to compare to, and from in there a loss looks exactly like a difference. An emulation saying that it is fine shows nothing, as it would say that either way.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#comparison-and-verification-problem

### Transformative experience

L. A. Paul's name for experiences, such as becoming a vampire or having a child, that one cannot judge from the outside beforehand. 7/30 uses it for the second reason to keep the baseline first: deciding for a new sense from the outside is like ordering from a menu in a language one does not speak, where the dish then also changes what one likes to eat. So if there is a sane place to decide such things from, it is a stable one, one step at a time.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#transformative-experience

### Experience machine

Robert Nozick's thought experiment. 7/30 links it to what people outside the field most often say about "being embodied in a computer simulation": that they would feel trapped. Most of them do not want new colours, but to stick around in their familiar environment, with their own place and their friends.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#experience-machine

### Collective mind

The third and last outcome of the Ontology (8/30). As soon as synthetic consciousness has been achieved via hybrid mind uploading, there is technically the possibility to merge into one giant collective mind, with one process world-line instead of "society", and phenomenally conscious as a whole, not only smart as a whole the way a society or the internet can be. Most transhumanists assume that they stay single individuals. 8/30 expects it to start occasionally, to show something instead of telling it, until coming apart again is the exception. Whether one would then still be around as oneself is left open.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#collective-mind

### Neurophenomenal structuralism

Holger Lyre's view, which 8/30 takes seriously: what an experience is like is fixed by its position in a structure of relations to all other experiences (the Q-structure), and how that position gets activated, by the eyes or by a memory, should not matter. That it obviously does matter, as a remembered sunset is pale next to the one in front of you, is what the January 2026 essay explains with ecphoric reconstruction.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#neurophenomenal-structuralism

### Ecphoric reconstruction

The name 8/30 uses for how a biological brain remembers: it keeps a compressed, lossy version of an experience (its engram) and rebuilds the rest from priors at recall. So remembering lands somewhere near the original position in the structure of experiences and never exactly on it. Take that bottleneck away on a substrate built without the compression constraint, and a memory would be the full experience again (lossless Q-storage), if that can be built at all.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#ecphoric-reconstruction

### Q-time and P-time

Two layers of time from the unpublished January 2026 essay. Q-time is personal, phenomenal time; P-time is substrate time, the physical time in which the substrate keeps moving forward like everything else. With a past that can be re-entered at full resolution, personal time turns from something one gets pushed through into something one can walk around in, like a DVD that can be rewound while the player does not get a day younger. The destruction of the forward arrow only ever happens in Q-time, and no dualism is implied: both stay within physics.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#q-time-and-p-time

### Branching identity

If one can go back into a past experiential state, one can also decide differently from there and see where it goes, so the history of what one has experienced stops being a simple line and turns into a graph with branches (a directed acyclic graph, a picture borrowed from Toby Ord). In 8/30 this is the intrapersonal, Q-time kind of hivemind: one substrate, one ongoing process, many of "me", and in P-time still exactly one person.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#branching-identity

### Distributed unification

An operational requirement of the Ontology: many nodes, one mind. A brain that gets replaced piece by piece is for a long time a mix of old tissue and new parts, and that mix has to be one mind the whole time and not two. If that can be done between the parts of one brain, 8/30 sees nothing in the method that would care whose skull the parts came from, which is why collective mind is an outcome and not a goal.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#distributed-unification

### Show, don't tell

How someone multiplies 17 × 24 in their head can at best be described, and even a much better description fails to carry over what it is like (Feynman and Tukey both "counted", in different ways, and only found out by trying). 8/30 connects this with Wittgenstein: what can be shown cannot be said, and the beetle in the box. Whatever turns experience into signals and back is still telling, only with more channels; the moment something really gets shown, there is a bit less of "two heads" than before.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#show-dont-tell

### Strong multiple realisability

The strong form of the Ontology's first requirement (9/30). Weak multiple realisability holds if engrams or functions get shifted around from living tissue to living tissue inside one brain, which the serial lesion effect and slowly growing low-grade gliomas show to some degree. The strong form holds if de novo tissue, tissue that was never part of that brain and maybe is not even biological, can also store and implement the same functions. If only living de novo tissue can, hybrid mind uploading has to go towards extreme biology.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#strong-multiple-realisability

### Operational and axiomatic requirements

A requirement is something that has to be true about brains for hybrid mind uploading to have a chance at all. The Ontology has four of each kind. The operational ones (multiple realisability, continuer migration, morphological independence, distributed unification) are things a brain turns out to be able to do or not, so an experiment can come back with a no, and each has a weak and a strong form. The axiomatic ones (brain-centredness, methodological physicalism, non-organicism, scale separation) have to be granted before any of those experiments means anything, so each is taken in its least committal form.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#operational-and-axiomatic-requirements

### Lesion momentum

The clinic's word for how fast a lesion grows, the variable that the gradual reorganisation principle hangs on. In rats ten days between two stages is too fast for a frontal cortex and twenty is enough; in people with low-grade gliomas about 4 mm a year is slow enough for speech and movement. In between there is apparently nothing, and 9/30 wants it as an actual measurement, a speed limit more accurate than "slower than a stroke".

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#lesion-momentum

### Grandmother's face problem

Slow lesions spare what is measurable from the outside, such as speech and motor function, which are retrieved all day long. But what about engrams that you are not aware of having until you recall them, such as the rarely retrieved memory of your grandmother's face? The only test for an engram is to retrieve it, and retrieving is an intervention that rehearses the trace and opens it up to change, so there is no baseline for the unmeasured ones, and forgetting does not feel like anything.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#grandmothers-face-problem

### Continuer migration

The second requirement of the Ontology (10/30). It is about how the move has to go so that it is still you who arrives, and its one particular word, the continuer, brings the entire philosophy of personal identity along. 10/30 sets the thought experiments aside: whether psychological or physical continuity carries you through, what matters is the continuity of the human brain, kept running so that no accident or disease robs you of it.

Source: https://consciousness.ink/glossary/#continuer-migration

---

## 0/30 Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness: The Start

URL: https://consciousness.ink/0-the-start/
Author: Daniel Burger
Published: 2026-11-11
Topics: synthetic consciousness, hybrid mind uploading, classical mind uploading, process world-line, gradual brain replacement, serial lesion effect, gradual reorganisation principle, solving death, immortality, theory of consciousness, world-line fidelity, continuer migration

On the first day of this year, I created a small ontology editor (similar to, e.g. Protégé, just a lot simpler and without the formal OWL logic behind it) for the all-encompassing ontology* of my life and its vision, mission, goals, etc. It starts with the main vision (i.e. the future state of being I'm working towards), which is "synthetic consciousness". Simply summarised: engineered phenomenology on a designed substrate you could gradually become. I break it down into the mission, which is hybrid mind uploading (the most pragmatic way to achieve the same goals as classical mind uploading, just not by following the free-standing position of "creating something external to the brain that recreates the brain" but rather by building something that can be integrated into the thing at hand (i.e. your brain), hence the hybrid status in between. If you read some of my recent tweets, you'll know what I mean, as I've been talking about it in great detail + there's the upcoming manuscript on it. Then there are a few principles and rejections, some goals, one of which is quite practical: solve death (more on this below), and a few other things.

Btw, in September I already listed most of the terms I keep using and explained them in relation to each other ( [Sep 2026] ), but that was more of a glossary where the terms just stand side by side, whereas the ontology is a tree and therefore also says what sits under what. The tree itself is very pragmatic on purpose (I don't add text if it's not necessary; every word has a "right to exist"), which obviously also means that pretty much all the actual arguments behind those few words are either in my head, in old tweets and threads, or in manuscripts that aren't finished yet, and that's not really of much use to anyone but me...

So, as quickly described yesterday, I'm at Inkhaven (at Lighthaven) for the next 30 days anyway, and the plan is to work through the ontology and discuss (nearly) every item under the synthetic consciousness vision in public, one per day, as a meditation. I call them meditations in the sense of Descartes (Husserl picked that up again later with his Cartesian Meditations, e.g.), i.e. I write them in the first person and step by step, showing my thought process during writing, so that others as readers can go through it by themselves and see how I get to something (wrong turns included, I'll leave them in!), rather than just having to believe me. This makes everything a bit messier, but I do actually enjoy reading meditations myself, so here we go!

In every one of the meditations, I want to do two things basically. Obviously I have to argue for whatever the item claims, as the tree itself only states things (remember, every word has a right to exist, so there are no real arguments in there). But I also want to check the words themselves, i.e. what they're even supposed to mean, because terms like "continuer migration" or "world-line fidelity" can very easily sound a lot deeper than they are (a very Wittgensteinian worry), and whatever doesn't survive that has to go from the ontology again.

Here is a simple example of what I mean by this, using the goals as stated above for "solve death": Death, as I use it, is the irreversible end of the process world-line, the process world-line being the 4D trajectory of the physical-dynamical and organised bounded processes going on in your head that constitute what we call your brain. Not subscribing to any particular theory of consciousness basically lets you work with what you have at hand, which is the human brain, i.e. the main empirical object of investigation. The process itself starts at birth (technically slightly earlier, tbd) and ends when you die – it's one continuous thing (the "continuous" part can ofc also be attacked philosophically, more on that on the day we discuss it!). Either way, the premise: death is a contingent failure of the substrate. The move: swap the substrate out piece by piece without destroying the physical-dynamical and organised bounded processes – while hopefully introducing repairability/fault tolerance – so that the process hardens and becomes more resilient (i.e. the hardening of the process world-line).

Now, what I can actually argue for today is that the one biological brain you have keeps ageing and is therefore a single point of failure (= easy), and also that a different piece of brain can take over a function, as there's the serial lesion effect and Barrett's (2013) gradual reorganisation principle for that. What neither of them gives you is a different substrate taking over though, which is still open and basically the reason for the whole replacement work of ours at @synconeticsorg (so no, I can't argue for that part today). Also, "solved" doesn't mean immortal => the limits go from biological to "purely" physical ones, and the universe has plenty of those (heat death, eventually), so immortality is really its own question. Which makes me wonder if "solve" is even the right word for this goal? No idea yet tbh, we'll see when we get to it.

So the commitment for the next 30 days is one item of the ontology per day, as a public meditation here on my Twitter. Btw, nothing here is final, and some of it will change, as both the September list and the tree (OG tweet retweeted here => the screenshot) already have outdated bits, and if an item doesn't survive its own meditation, I'll rename it or throw it out and update the tree accordingly.

Tomorrow it's 1/30, which is the vision itself => synthetic consciousness! :-)

* PS: The term "ontology" might not be perfect or 100% correct here, it might be more of a taxonomy (or simply a hierarchy), i.e. from broad to small and well-defined, which is how the current version in my self-made editor works. However, I'd love to turn it more into a "what exists within a domain, plus the interconnections/relationships between those things and what follows from those relationships" (i.e. a proper ontology)

---

## 1/30 Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness: Causa Finalis

URL: https://consciousness.ink/1-causa-finalis/
Author: Daniel Burger
Published: 2026-11-12
Topics: synthetic consciousness, hybrid mind uploading, classical mind uploading, process world-line, solving death, deprivation view of death, substrate independence

The first item in my Ontology (as discussed yesterday, with an uppercase "O" to denote "my ontology as discussed yesterday," rather than a lowercase "o" for any ontology or the general concept itself) is the "future state of being" => that's the entity "Vision", i.e. a state (as opposed to a way of getting there) that doesn't hold yet. Within the Ontology it's the "causa finalis", i.e. the end every other item in there is done for (the "that for the sake of which"), with no claim that it's the highest good: nothing matters except to someone conscious, and ordinary biological consciousness already meets that condition. So the end this Ontology is ordered to is that no consciousness has to end, and synthetic consciousness is that end as a state of being: consciousness that no longer has to end (the vision), and the route to it is hybrid mind uploading (the mission). Or, to put all of that in one line (which is basically today's whole meditation already): consciousness is the reason why its end matters at all, the world-line is the thing that actually has to continue, and "synthetic" is just there to say that the result is the real kind via a creation process. So I want to have synthetic consciousness (what exactly the term commits me to follows below) reached and then kept in the – hopefully near – future.

Now, what is "synthetic consciousness"? It's definitely not as common a term as e.g. artificial consciousness, as the term "artificial" is arguably (as you can assume) generally more widely spread due to e.g. artificial intelligence being as prominent as it is right now. That's actually also the reason for "artificial consciousness" being used more broadly for a bunch of things: the consciousness an AI system might have, the research field that studies it, and within that field two different aims known as weak and strong artificial consciousness (e.g. [arxiv.org] ), i.e. modelling the mechanisms of consciousness in software/robots without claiming that anything is experiencing anything vs building something that actually is conscious. I bring this up, as the term on its own doesn't tell you whether the real thing is meant, and "synthetic consciousness" gets listed as just another name for it, as on Wikipedia ( [en.wikipedia.org] ), which is not how I use it, hence both words need their justification here. (And yes, there's also the adjacent term "machine consciousness", which I'll come to below, along with why "synthetic")

When choosing the word (or words) for the causa finalis, I wanted the "fewest words possible", as each word has to have a pragmatic right to exist and each additional one adds a certain attack surface. Hence I for sure started with "consciousness" as the term, and only later added "synthetic". I deliberately wanted to use "consciousness". From a physical perspective you might say, well, some fields or strings might be the most fundamental thing in the universe, and they might be => consciousness isn't necessarily the most fundamental thing in the universe, but it's the most fundamental thing to anyone in it. So no matter what the universe is ultimately made of, consciousness is the one thing I just can't doubt I have (or at least as the Descartes' Meditations have it: "ego sum, ego existo") and it's also the one thing without which nothing in the universe would matter to anyone. This only certifies the present though, meaning that I am right now, and it doesn't say anything about me going on => what carries the going-on is the world-line. And once consciousness is gone for good, nothing shows up for you ever again, and I think losing it is "bad" exactly because of everything it cuts you off from (that's Nagel's deprivation view btw, as opposed to Epicurus with his "death is nothing to us"). That's why its end is the thing worth solving, and also why the vision is about consciousness – and not e.g. about intelligence or life.

So "consciousness" was chosen by me for the term of the vision. Well, I can't just have "consciousness" as a vision (too simple, kind of defeats the whole point, too reductionistic), so it needs another term next to it for sure, and I don't want to use a neologism for that. Why "synthetic" as the first term then, and not e.g. "artificial" or "machine" as talked about before? That depends on what the vision actually is. My vision is that consciousness, starting with the consciousness that exists now, still exists in the future. However, consciousness as it is today, biological and "original", has one defect that matters here: it has to end. It's not the most durable state we can have (again, more on that below).

Generally, I care because I made it my life's mission ≈10 years ago to solve death. Solve death, meaning what? What is death? Without going too much into detail prematurely, as this is one of the goals of the Ontology (as e.g. written about yesterday), I want to put it simply: death is the irreversible end of a conscious world-line. That can be read in two ways though, and the two need to be kept apart, as they're two different problems. Global death: no conscious observers are left anywhere, so death rules the universe if there's no life, or at least no conscious observer, in the future. Individual death: this consciousness ends, i.e. one person's process world-line stops irreversibly. That's the one people actually fear, since for the one who dies it's the end of a world and not one event in a world that goes on ("at death the world does not alter, but comes to an end", Wittgenstein's Tractatus 6.431, btw!).

So, back to the vision: I want consciousness to still be in a future state, so no death, but focusing on my death, and yours (not deaths, not statistics in the sense of statistical likelihood of death occurring being reduced, not multiple consciousnesses, etc.). It's about individual death first. A resilient new mind that begins when I die doesn't achieve the vision => the vision is the conjunction, consciousness goes on and this consciousness goes on, and neither part satisfies it alone. Solve individual death from its first principles and, I'll argue, you end up with what I now call "hybrid mind uploading", and not classical copy-based uploading (that's the mission's day of the meditations challenge).

And on what day could I say death is solved? If the test is "death can no longer occur in the universe", then never (any structure can be destroyed, and there's heat death), a goal no one could ever check off. So I move the "must": today everyone has to die, and solved means no one has to end (some will choose not to continue, and things can still go wrong). Death goes from a certainty to a risk, and a risk is something you can measure and work on, although it has to keep falling, and fast enough, as a constant risk, however small, still gets everyone in the limit; it has to fall fast enough that all the yearly risks together add up to a finite total (sleep e.g., and the harder cases (e.g. hypothermic arrest), belong to the day on the 4D process world-line).

There are two approaches to keeping consciousness from ending. One is to make the default top-of-the-pyramid conscious thing (i.e. humans) fault tolerant as a species. Basically what Musk is after => replicate humanity across initially two planets in the same solar system, and obviously across more moons and planets soon, in order to increase fault tolerance through redundancy => if Earth dies or gets destroyed, we at least have a bunch of backups. But his vision doesn't say how consciousness is preserved in any more detailed manner, meaning he's fine if someone, and hopefully as many as possible, is around. I think this is great, his route is a real one. So in the global sense Musk is also a "solve death" person, but slightly different, he makes us fault tolerant as a species, and with that the chance of total death occurring (= no conscious observers) gets smaller, statistically speaking, but he's not focused on the first principles of death itself, which is what kept me busy a few years back. He's right, he just answers a different question: keeping some consciousness around is not the same as keeping this consciousness going. And this goes the other way around too, as ending individual death doesn't entail the end of global death. Undying minds that all live on one planet still die with the planet (you'd need the premise that no single event can end every world-line at once), so Musk's route is not my alternative, I need it as well – or at least wish for it in parallel!

The other approach goes at consciousness itself. The requirements of the vision, and its goals and opportunities, require things of consciousness that today's biology can't provide. Biological consciousness is first of all quite fragile, hence not resilient, meaning it can vanish quite fast in the first-principles view, as in, it's so easy to die, and for death to occur, in this universe. So the question becomes, how to make consciousness more resilient? Well, you can go into hardening things (borrowed terminology from software engineering), meaning can you harden biological consciousness? Can you fight against entropy as some people call it? If you go down that avenue of thought, as I did a couple of years ago (coming from classical mind uploading, as I was philosophically more naive back then), you most likely end up with the same conclusion as younger Daniel, which is "whatever state of consciousness you want to have and preserve, it needs to be some sort of hardened and therefore non-natural/initial-state consciousness in the future". And that's where I think most people go into terminologies such as "resilient consciousness", or one further, "substrate-independent consciousness", which implies fault tolerance in the substrate and an easy distribution across locations and easy transfer from one substrate to the other, and a bunch of other things (an assumption I think is untested; more on its own day in the challenge). Or you settle indeed with "well, if we can engineer consciousness (as some argue, even without understanding it), then we can potentially create de novo consciousness, with all of its implications".

So, what is this hardened de novo consciousness? Biological consciousness engineered to last, or consciousness re-created somewhere, in either a biological brain or maybe something non-biological, as substrate independence e.g. implies? Follow this logic and you end up somewhere funny (it's a reductio, to be clear – of the idea that new + hardened is enough): technically you can, based on that reasoning, come to the same conclusion as Musk, that creating biological consciousness in a hardened, de novo way is actually just giving birth to it. The best way to create de novo hardened consciousness is to have a baby (de novo in that context meaning it's newly created, independent of your consciousness or any other consciousness + it's hardened, because it's young, with little accumulated damage). So you indeed end up with the same reasoning as Musk, so why care? Well, it's hardened, but not really, and above all it's new: a baby is a new world-line and not the continuation of anyone's, so by going into a generational approach you never touch individual death. De novo + hardened isn't enough, as a newborn already meets both and solves nothing => what's missing is continuity, the same world-line made resilient. So, if you focus on the first principles of death (this consciousness ending, and not just some consciousness being around), you need this hardened de novo substrate to indeed be more engineered. So from here on, "de novo" means the substrate only: a designed substrate, and the consciousness on it is the one that's already there, a process that could come to run on it gradually (argued on the mission's day tomorrow).

So, it's artificial? In one sense yes, in the sense that matters no. What does artificial even mean? It goes back to the Latin artificium (craft or skill), so made by art or skill and not by nature, and in that sense an engineered substrate obviously is artificial. But the word has come to mean made in imitation of something natural, a substitute (artificial flowers, artificial sweetener, etc.), and the important part here is "it's not the thing it imitates". I don't want to have, as a future vision/state of being, a bunch of "not real consciousness" around, so I had issues calling the top-most item in the Ontology "artificial consciousness". So why not use what many people have started using, which is "machine consciousness" as mentioned earlier? Well, I have my tail of issues with the term "machine", as it implies we're creating a machine (which isn't true per se, or at least I don't want to imply it already from day 1), but it also invites the reading that a mind is something you can lift out and move into another machine that we engineer. And that's basically computational functionalism, to a certain degree already frontloaded, which is one of the three positions I reject (each of them gets its own day in the meditations challenge), so I really can't have it baked into the name of the vision.

So, what term is the right one? Well, after years of thought I settled on "synthetic" => take sugar. If you make sucrose in a lab (which was first done in 1953), you still end up with sucrose, so the very same molecule, just made via another route, whereas an artificial sweetener like e.g. aspartame is a totally different molecule that only mimics the sweetness. So for me, synthetic means the same kind of thing, but just made by another route. And artificial means an imitation of the thing (e.g. Herbert Simon draws pretty much the same line with gems in "The Sciences of the Artificial" btw, and yes, everyday usage is messier, as synthetic leather obviously isn't leather, so I mean it the way e.g. chemists would use the word).

Now, this of course commits me to synthetic consciousness being the same kind as biological consciousness, so real and not an imitation, and to be clear, that's what the vision hopes for, and nothing that the word itself could ever establish. With sugar you have the chemistry, and with a diamond you have its lattice structure to "show and validate" that it's indeed the same kind. But what plays that exact role for consciousness? That's a question of scale separability as well as coarse graining and indeed a thing we should talk about as well (and as long as that's open, "real" is more of a wish than a description, so I still owe that answer on a later day of the challenge too...). So, meaning, that for now I actually only use "synthetic" as a term for "the real kind" – independently of how it is produced/created. The word specifies the target, but the question if that target can actually be reached, remains an open question to be answered. Additionally, the word only names the kind. As an example: sucrose from the lab is a new molecule and not the old one that somehow got "carried over", which means that the word alone cannot tell you that "a synthetic new me" is still "me", even though I use "synthetic" and not "artificial" (as that part has to come from the process worldline).

To conclude for now: This future state of being, as the "root and start" of the Ontology (first in intention, last in execution, as Aquinas puts it) labelled as the entity "Vision" (its root node or causa finalis: the end everything else in the Ontology is done for) has a bunch of implications and relations, as already hinted at earlier, which the coming days take up one by one.

– – –

fn1: Of course, the sugar analogy relies on experience itself, as sweetness only has meaning to someone who has tasted it. But with all of philosophy running via language, and language being used by conscious observers who actually have experience of e.g. things such as sweetness, this analogy still holds when it comes to the terminology itself, as in, when trying to give things a term while being a conscious observer, a terminology that acts as if nobody is doing the naming just doesn't make sense to me, even though the thing that a term picks out (e.g. the sucrose molecule) of course doesn't have to depend on anybody (it's "aphilosophical"/"unphilosophical", if you like)

fn2: This one is just a nice coincidence of words btw, and no argument at all: in phenomenology, consciousness is already a synthesis by itself, as every moment still holds the one that just passed and already reaches for the next one (Husserl even calls synthesis the "Urform" of consciousness, see §17 of his Cartesian Meditations), so the word "synthetic" kind of fits the thing itself too, and not only the way it's made

fn3: Most people know it as "cogito, ergo sum", but the Meditations themselves actually have it as "ego sum, ego existo", so without the "ergo", and that's exactly the version I need here => it's evident every single time I think it, and there's no syllogism behind it with a premise that somebody could attack, which is also what Descartes himself says in the Second Replies (AT VII 140)

---

## 2/30 Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness: What Could Be Hybrid about Mind Uploading?

URL: https://consciousness.ink/2-hybrid-mind-uploading/
Author: Daniel Burger
Published: 2026-11-13
Topics: synthetic consciousness, hybrid mind uploading, classical mind uploading, mind uploading, whole brain emulation, process world-line, solving death, immortality, limits of biology, substrate independence

The next item in the Ontology is the mission, which, as I understand and use it, is the undertaking that leads to the vision (and "hybrid mind uploading" is its name), with the vision being a state of being in the future described as "there will be synthetic consciousness", as discussed in great detail yesterday ( [Nov 2026] ). One thing became quite clear yesterday: you cannot define a single item in the Ontology without first defining its relations to other items, which makes linear-style writing in a left-to-right language such as English quite hard without anticipating some of the other items in the Ontology. The one already mentioned was hybrid mind uploading.

It seems that, in order not to stay with naturally produced consciousness, due to all the things discussed yesterday (it's fragile, hence not resilient, and above all it has to end), but in order to go into a new state that is meant to continue the same process world-line, just no longer naturally produced, therefore "'something' consciousness", for which we used the term "synthetic" as in "the same kind, but created/engineered", the great focus has to be on the "well, what is the process?".

Over the past few years, I've been slowly coming out of the field of (classical) mind uploading ( [Dec 2023] , [Mar 2026] , and, as the final push, [Nov 2026] ). After I had defined it to be my life's mission to solve death (as described yesterday), I first thought that the most pragmatic way is to focus on consciousness as the most fundamental thing, and then try to preserve that with the most resilience and upshots to other things ("opportunities", as I called them yesterday), and that this would be mind uploading: scan a brain in as much detail as possible, store it somewhere and then simulate it in order to emulate consciousness on a different substrate, hence a computer. This is what I define as "classical mind uploading" nowadays, btw. So I was never technically interested in other forms of rejuvenation or gene therapies, because they don't focus on the first principles of death; they keep the process world-line within the limits of biology, and they don't address the full range of vulnerabilities I want to overcome.

Now, the problem with this classical approach as described before, as some of you might know if you've been following me on Twitter in the past few years (e.g. [Sep 2026] and [Sep 2026] ), is that there are a bunch of issues, which I do not want to repeat again (I once called it "dying with extra steps": [Aug 2025] ), especially because those rejections and criticisms are actually other Ontology items for the daily meditations challenge in the coming days.

The important story background here is that at some point, I wanted to distance myself completely from the "mind uploading" term, as I saw all the issues and wasn't even a fan of the terminology of "mind" and "uploading" on its own. What is a mind? What is uploading? (I'll keep both words for now btw, and the first question gets its answer in a later meditation) Uploading is so frontloaded with computer science terminology, and to be fair, a term that's borrowed from another discipline isn't a problem by itself; it only becomes one when its familiar use quietly decides what has to be true in the new discipline as well, so in the minds of the researchers and people (Wittgenstein style again). I was obviously not the first person to have issues with this; afaik @randalkoene had similar concerns, and around 1998 he named the academic approach "whole brain emulation". "Mind uploading" came down from the Hans Moravec lineage, front-loaded with even more sci-fi connotations, which might be a net negative for a scientific, serious discipline.

Now, I thought that "whole brain emulation" is a great term (Randal Koene later also used "substrate-independent minds" btw), so I was looking into terming the mission with something around it, e.g. candidates such as "invariant brain emulation" ( [Jun 2025] ), in order to imply other aspects of the Ontology, e.g. that the thing we want to recreate has no self-standing position, but actually integrates into the brain at hand, and also that the process world-line doesn't break, and other things (as late as April this year I still called myself "a WBE person, but not via simulations": [Apr 2026] ). But I had a few issues with that. Why WHOLE? What does this mean? It already implies "just" the brain to a certain degree; therefore, some degree of brain-centredness of consciousness, which might be too much of a leap of faith already. Also, brain? Why just the brain? Even more brain-centredness (and yes, I'm aware that the slide in my own Ontology says "make the brain hybrid", but the brain is where we start, and that's no claim about where consciousness has to live). And emulation? Emulation is, I guess, an even worse ambiguous term than uploading, because emulation is mostly understood as JUST a software term (which it doesn't have to be btw: [Jun 2025] ), and based on my own experience it's actually sometimes used interchangeably with simulation. So I ran into a few issues with terming this mission item in the Ontology.

After a few years, I basically realised, especially when starting to pitch this to a few people, friends, investors, that using a neologism is bad, as it's front-loaded with too much abstraction. I always admired pitches of people who could just use "XYZ but for XYZ", so using something familiar and then mapping it, e.g. onto your problem space. At some point, I remember, I realised that actually "mind uploading" is a great term, as it implies, even for most people who are not in the space at all, things such as "immortality, solving death, mind augmentation and enabling a new state of humanity" and a few more. I liked that, after all. And before somebody calls that a double standard, as "uploading" is obviously a computer science term too: I keep the word for what it promises, and I drop its old method, meaning that with hybrid mind uploading I don't mean reconstructing a separate instance somewhere and then treating that copy as my survival.

But I did not like the immediate association with mind uploading being a subdiscipline of computer science and nowadays AI, and that it's mostly, and nearly only if you look at the literature (look at previous posts here: [Sep 2026] and here: [Sep 2026] ), used for "scan, store, simulate" => all engineering efforts are within "recreating a self-standing brain from brain scans, sometimes even fully destructive". So the process world-line discussion rarely came up, and never at the centre, and the aspect of knowing if a simulation will be sufficient for a full emulation, or if it's even able to have phenomenal consciousness, is a recurring issue (e.g. [Feb 2026] , and something more to discuss in the meditation where I'll discuss the Synconetics programme in the coming days).

So I thought of "moving the original goals of mind uploading, which are solving death, mind augmentation and enabling a new state of humanity", as e.g. popularised in the Hans Moravec lineage (Moravec's own robot-surgeon procedure in "Mind Children" from 1988 was already a gradual one btw, but its end state was still the mind as a computer program), from it being a subdiscipline of CS and AI into a discipline(s) with fewer metaphysical claims and assumptions (so fewer metaphysical commitments, and ones that experiments can at least bear on, and not zero, as the process world-line is still one of them), and to make the remaining assumptions explicit and investigate them, instead of taking leaps of faith ( [Oct 2025] , and for the functionalism part of it [Apr 2026] and [Jul 2026] ). So I denoted whatever mind uploading via whole brain emulation used to be as "classical mind uploading", and whatever is new as "XYZ mind uploading".

Now the question was: what term to use for XYZ? As the idea (one of many ideas, as you will see in the coming days as well) is to go through/via a hybrid state of the thing that carries the process world-line into the synthetic consciousness state as the causa finalis, we will enter a hybrid state on the way from whatever was the starting point (i.e. biologically sustained consciousness) to the end state (synthetically sustained consciousness). Hence: hybrid ( [Jul 2026] ). And to answer the question from the title as well: by "hybrid" I mean that biological and engineered parts are carrying one and the same process at the same time, so the thing that is hybrid is what carries the consciousness, and never the consciousness itself (so please don't picture some "half-synthetic" experience here, as synthetic means the same kind, see yesterday). It's actually that simple. And by "process world-line" I mean a physical claim about the process itself that does the carrying, and not a report of "how continuous it feels" => as a copy would feel continuous too! And if this particular consciousness really gets preserved via that transition is the aim of the whole mission, and nothing that the word "hybrid" could establish by itself (if the hybrid state is only a passage, or if somebody could also just stay hybrid, is a question for another day as well). But for today I can only say this: I call the consciousness "synthetic" once it's sustained by created and engineered parts, and whether the hybrid state already counts as that is exactly the question I'm leaving open (at least for now).

What this all implies, and all the issues that I have with classical mind uploading, and what assumptions and axioms we still have in hybrid mind uploading, is part of the Ontology when we go down in more detail, and therefore part of another day (and for those who can't wait: the post distinguishing classical from hybrid [Mar 2026] , the river as the border between the two [May 2026] , "The Alien Neuron" [Sep 2026] , and why it's harder than classical, but better [Oct 2026] ).

---

## 3/30 Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness: Solving Death

URL: https://consciousness.ink/3-solving-death/
Author: Daniel Burger
Published: 2026-11-14
Topics: synthetic consciousness, hybrid mind uploading, process world-line, gradual brain replacement, mechanistic gradual brain replacement, solving death, functional brain isolation, deprivation view of death, adaptive preferences, genetic fallacy, death, amortality, immortality

I run a company called @eightsixscience , where we try to functionally isolate the brain ( [Sep 2026] ); in other words, we take living brains out of their bodies and keep them alive outside their original bodies for as long as possible. We have early success in doing so in rodents; we're working toward the same for a large-animal brain, and ultimately we want to do this for humans as well. When I tell people about this – friends, family, people I meet at scientific conferences, investors or also just random people I meet throughout life (e.g. my hairdresser, who I recently told what exactly I'm doing) – I usually get the one question that gets asked most: "Why are you doing this?" I simply answer: "Because I want to solve death, and functionally isolating brains is, according to my own reasoning, the most pragmatic route towards that goal". And then usually the question comes right after: "But, why? Why do you want to solve death?"

The short answer, before I ramble on for way too long: it's complicated, and no, I still don't have a clean one after ≈10 years of getting asked. I can tell you why death is bad for the one who dies; that part I'm fairly sure about. But why exactly me, why I can't put this thing down again? No idea, and it gets worse the longer I think about it – same as with "what has to be true along the way" as well as "when would we even call it solved"; because every time I answer one of those, I do actually end up with a new question instead: what even is a world-line, what makes a continuation worth having, and so on (which is btw exactly why solving death is one of the three hard goals that the mission has to achieve in the Ontology).

Depending on who asks, I've come to several answers over the years, depending on the person, the context, and the time available. It ranges from personal upbringing reasons, e.g. my mom going through the Yugoslav wars and telling me stories as a child about all the terrible things that she had seen (hence developing a morbid and catastrophic view on death early on), or that I was depressed as a teenager and prob read the wrong kinds of books in a row that led me, back then, towards thinking that death is actually the only answer (that phase is long over btw). Now, the thing is, and I have to be strict with myself here, that both of these stories answer a question that nobody asked. When somebody asks me "why do you want this?", they could mean "what made you want it?" or they could mean "what makes it worth wanting?". Those are actually two very different things => the first one is a cause and the second one a reason (and my mom's stories and my teenage bookshelf are e.g. obv causes). They tell you how I ended up with death as my main topic. But if the goal itself is any good: they don't tell you at all (and tbh, they also can't tell you that it's bad. People do try that one, and it's the genetic fallacy, just used in the other direction!). The usual comeback here is "so it's just your fear of death talking", and I think that one deserves an honest answer: yes, maybe, I even posted a quote once saying that one of the principal things that moves people is the terror of death ( [Oct 2024] ). But you can play the exact same game with the other side! For basically all of human history there was nothing, like really nothing, that anybody could do about it, so what else would you do other than making your peace with it (Elster calls this adaptive preferences, or just "sour grapes"). So fine, my wish can be explained away, but so can everybody else's acceptance, and then explaining away doesn't decide anything here.

Other avenues of explanation are usually more mythological, as in: death always seemed to be humanity's forbidden fruit and life in general; it's the one great barrier one shall not pass, and if you're curious, you obviously love to explore that boundary. Again, curiosity is a cause and no reason, but the "shall not pass" part deserves a closer look, as nearly every culture has a story that warns you about going there (e.g. Gilgamesh loses his plant of youth to a snake, and Tithonus gets his eternal life without the eternal youth). Even my own "forbidden fruit" picture fits btw, as in Genesis the forbidden fruit is strictly speaking knowledge, and it's the tree of life that gets guarded afterwards, so that nobody eats from it and lives forever. People sometimes hand me these stories as an argument, as in "humanity has always known that this is a bad idea". I read them as the wisdom of a time in which nothing could be done, so they belong to the same making-peace as above, and if you look closely, what most of them warn against is a bad version of not having to die (ageing forever, being alone forever), which nobody is asking for. The one reading that's left is the hubris one, that it's against the order of things, and "the order of things" is no argument by itself, as the night is part of that order as well, which brings me to the lightbulbs.

So, more societally as an explanation, one of the analogies I've recently been bringing up during conversations is the example of pitching the lightbulb in front of people working on candles in the early 1800s. Instead of accepting the limitations of candles for brightening up the night, which is what we've done for thousands of years as Homo sapiens, why not go beyond those limits by inventing magically glowing things called lightbulbs, whose light doesn't have to burn down the way a candle does? It's coming from a totally different angle to solve the same problem, which is: keep it bright for as long as you want (you see the analogies I'm drawing slowly creeping in!). When working on lightbulbs, you don't iterate on candles; you approach it with different things. And that's the beauty, because the upshot of solving "it being bright at night, against nature's reason to make it dark at night due to the earth blocking the sunlight" is that we ultimately needed to work on electricity, have constant access to electricity, DC then AC, and this led towards the electrification of a bunch of things, and ultimately also to the digital computer, and then AI, AGI and superintelligence (quite literally btw: the "Edison effect" was found inside a lightbulb in the early 1880s, Fleming turned it into the first vacuum tube in 1904, and the first electronic computers were rooms full of the descendants of that tube). Who would have thought that the people working on lightbulbs back in the day were working on this uphill technology with a tail that leads us towards superintelligence? I usually say that solving death kind of feels like this nowadays. It seems like, for the first time, we have enough of the technology and knowledge to start seriously, so let's try. The upshot of this is unknown, and nobody can predict it; we can only guess. A few people like Nikola Tesla predicted, quite accurately, some future scenarios back then, but I don't think this is possible anymore, and I don't know anything about what the future has in store for us when we solve death, other than that solving death is just step one and that life in a post-death society will be stranger than we can imagine ( [Oct 2025] ).

I used to end this pitch with "but whatever it is, it must be net positive, otherwise it will be filtered out either way" (basically "dialectic" in society), and I have to take that part back, as it doesn't survive my own scrutiny. Bad things can stick around for a very long time before a society filters them out, and some things do the filtering on us instead. So let me say what I think the analogy really gives me. It shows the kind of move, as the improvement path of the candle (better wax, better wicks) never arrives at the lightbulb, and the candle here is biology. You can make it burn longer, and I'm all for that, but, e.g. reversing ageing halts the dying and doesn't solve death, as you can still get hit by a bus ( [Sep 2026] ). It also shows that the upshots came through the infrastructure that the solution needed (electricity), which nobody working on it could foresee, and I expect the same here, as you can't work on this without understanding and engineering the thing that carries consciousness. And it takes care of the "order of things" from above, as nobody thinks today that the lightbulb was an offence against the night. Now, does any of this tell me that the result will be good? No, and no analogy ever could; I mean, it's lightbulbs. And there's one place where my nice analogy just falls apart, and it's kind of the most important place => continuity. If a lightbulb is off and you swap it for a new one, nobody cares; the light is simply "on again". With a consciousness, that's the whole difference between going on and being replaced (the 4D process world-line gets its own day). And what's left of my "it must be net positive" is weaker; I'm afraid => the direct effect is good if death is bad for the one who dies (next paragraph), and for everything that comes after that, I really don't know.

Now, to come back, I technically have even more examples, and they range from the personal "life is great, death is bad, so I want more of life" to the very logical reasons as described in one of the earlier meditations ( [Nov 2026] ), to the very visionary views such as the lightbulb scenario above. Out of these, the logical one is the one that carries the most weight for me (it's the central reason, if you want), so I'll go through it once more, slowly. It starts with the thing from day one => nothing matters except to someone conscious. Death is the irreversible end of a conscious process world-line, so when such a world-line ends, everything that would have come after just doesn't happen for the someone that this world-line is, and if that would have been worth having, then missing out on it is bad for that someone (that's Nagel's deprivation view; I didn't invent this). The "worth having" matters a lot btw, as it's the reason why the goal in the Ontology says "no one has to end" and why it never said, "no one is allowed to end". Also, yes, there are some well-known objections (e.g. Epicurus, Lucretius, "death gives life its meaning", "we have to make room", and so on, etc.), but I'll potentially talk about those things on another day, especially as today's meditation is getting way too long already...

OK, so that's the "why-is-death-bad"-part, and I think it holds up. But did you notice? I still haven't answered the question, as "why is death bad" and "why do YOU want to solve it" are just two different questions, and the second one is so much harder, which is kind of the main thing that I want to deliver today. A person can have every reason in their hands and yet still not know exactly why they actually want it. Arguments don't make people magically want things (on that part, Hume was right!). Plenty of people nod at every single step above and then go on with their lives as if nothing happened. So why do I want to solve death? Well, I don't know. Personal urge? I guess this is where the causes from the beginning come back in, as the reason is there for everybody, and my mom's stories and the wrong books are why I'm one of the people who can't put it down again. To put it simply: I will try doing so, otherwise I'll die either way, so who cares? That last part might sound like a joke, but I think there's actually a real argument hiding in it. Say nothing changes => I die, like everybody before me, that's the baseline. Say I try, and it doesn't work out => I die as well, so the same thing, except that there's whatever the attempt produced along the way. And if I try and it does work (for me, I mean), then that's obviously better, and if it only works for the people after me, then it's a gain for them and none for me, I'm aware of that. So for me, as far as I can see, trying is at least as good as not trying. There are two "buts" though. The attempt shouldn't cost me a life that I'd rather have lived (it doesn't – I love this work), and nothing worse than simply dying should be reachable along the way, and that second one doesn't come for free, nothing guarantees it, somebody has to design for it blabla. I know of two such outcomes on my own route btw. A conscious brain that's kept going without any input, without any way to act and without anything that protects it from suffering would be one of them, and I'd call that worse than death (more on that below). The other one is a "solution" that only produces a copy, or something that merely behaves like me, which people would walk into believing that they'd go on, and which is the reason why I only want engineering means that need no metaphysical gambling ( [Nov 2025] ), as that would be worse than no solution at all.

"Solving death" is one of the three goals of the Ontology ( [Sep 2026] ), and with the above in place I can say more exactly what it implies. The Ontology has a vision (synthetic consciousness, so consciousness that no longer has to end, which is a state), a mission (hybrid mind uploading, which is the undertaking) and the goals, which are what the mission has to achieve. Now, somebody who read day one carefully could say: wait, isn't "solving death" just the vision again, in other words? I asked myself the same, and I think it isn't, and the easiest way to see it is this => imagine that there's exactly one synthetic consciousness around, and everybody else still dies like today. Then you'd have a first instance of the vision, and you'd be nowhere near the goal. So with the vision, I'm talking about a state that should exist at all, and with the goal, I mean every single someone: your world-line doesn't have to end, and neither does anybody else's.
